question: What is the main job of the vital centres in your body?
explanation: You don't have to think about breathing or your heart beating! Vital centres run these automatic survival tasks behind the scenes. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h1)

question: Why is brainstem damage usually more life-threatening than an injury to the cerebral cortex?

options.A: The cerebral cortex can easily take over brainstem functions if needed
options.B: Brainstem tissue has a much slower rate of cellular regeneration
options.C: The brainstem houses autonomic centres controlling breathing and heart rate
options.D: Blood supply to the brainstem is much lower than to the cortex

explanation: Think of the brainstem as the master power switch for survival. Since it controls breathing and heart rate, any damage there puts immediate life support at risk. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h1)

question: Which part of the brainstem contains the main control hubs for heart rate and breathing rhythms?
explanation: The medulla oblongata is like the engine room of your brain, keeping your heart beating and your lungs breathing smoothly. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h2)

question: A patient has an injury mainly affecting the pons. What kind of breathing pattern would you expect to see?

options.A: Complete and immediate cessation of all lung movement
options.B: Inability to cough up mucus from the airway
options.C: Irregular transitions between inhaling and exhaling
options.D: Loss of conscious control over speaking while breathing

explanation: The pons helps smooth out the breathing rhythm set by the medulla. When it's injured, breathing can look a bit choppy and irregular. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h2)

question: Which cranial nerve sends signals from the brain to slow down the heart rate?
explanation: The vagus nerve is the body's main brake pedal, using parasympathetic signals to help calm and slow down the heart. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h3)

question: When a patient suddenly stands up and feels dizzy from a drop in blood pressure, how does the body normally respond?

options.A: Increases parasympathetic output to slow the heart right down
options.B: Triggers sympathetic vasoconstriction and increases heart rate
options.C: Shuts down vasomotor tone to pool blood in the lower limbs
options.D: Signals the respiratory centre to stop breathing temporarily

explanation: To stop you from fainting, your cardiovascular centre quickly tightens up your blood vessels and speeds up your heart to push blood back up to your brain! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h3)

question: What is the primary job of the Dorsal Respiratory Group in the medulla?

options.A: Triggering active exhalation during heavy exercise
options.B: Driving the basic automatic rhythm of inhalation
options.C: Controlling voluntary speech patterns during breathing
options.D: Detecting blood oxygen levels directly in the lungs

explanation: The dorsal respiratory group acts as the natural pacemaker for normal, quiet breathing so you don't have to think about every breath. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h4)

question: Why does the ventral respiratory group kick in when someone starts exercising hard?

options.A: To slow down the breathing rate and conserve energy
options.B: To drive forceful exhalation and deeper breaths required by the exertion
options.C: To bypass the damaged pons and restore normal speech
options.D: To cool down the brainstem through rapid airflow

explanation: Quiet breathing is mostly about inhaling, but heavy exercise requires extra effort. That's when the ventral group steps in to help you breathe out forcefully. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h4)

question: What does the brain's central chemoreceptor primarily monitor to control breathing?

options.A: Total volume of blood pumped per minute by the left ventricle
options.B: Concentration of glucose dissolved in blood plasma
options.C: Direct measurements of iron levels in circulating red blood cells
options.D: Changes in pH and carbon dioxide levels in cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Central chemoreceptors act like chemical sensors, checking the fluid around the brain for pH and carbon dioxide to decide how fast you need to breathe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h5)

question: Why does a patient with too much carbon dioxide in their body (hypercapnia) naturally start breathing much faster and deeper?

options.A: High carbon dioxide lowers fluid pH, strongly stimulating the respiratory centres
options.B: Excess carbon dioxide blocks parasympathetic signals to the heart
options.C: The brain detects the warm temperature of the gas and reacts
options.D: Carbon dioxide physically irritates the lining of the lungs and airways

explanation: When carbon dioxide builds up, it makes body fluids more acidic. This acid tickles the brain's breathing sensors, forcing the body to blow off the extra gas. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a classic sign of Cushing's triad when the brainstem is squeezed?

options.B: Persistent tachycardia with rapid weak pulses

explanation: Cushing's triad features a slow heart rate (bradycardia), not tachycardia, along with a wide pulse pressure and weird breathing patterns. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h6)

question: A patient takes too much of an opioid pain medication and their breathing drops to just 4 breaths per minute. Why does this happen?

options.A: Cerebral cortex voluntarily suppressing the urge to breathe
options.B: Peripheral muscles failing to respond to normal nerve signals
options.C: Medullary respiratory centres suppressed by circulating drug molecules
options.D: Carotid baroreceptors shutting off blood flow to the lungs

explanation: Opioids can bind to the brainstem and quiet down the breathing center so much that it forgets to signal the body to breathe at a normal rate. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T14#GNS211_U3_T14_h6)
